This work was supported by the Ministry University of Research (MUR), project CAI4DSA of FAIR PE1. ABSTRACT Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing by offering
human-like responses. However, issues such as incorrect information (hallucinations) and errors in specific
subject areas remain, especially in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. This study introduces
a Context-Aware Retrieval Augmented Generation (CA-RAG), which simplifies the process by removing
the need to separately find relevant chunks of a document. Instead, after dividing the document into
chunks, both the question and chunks are directly given to the LLMs to produce answers. The method then
focuses on improving the answers through additional post-processing, aiming to reduce errors and make the
answers more relevant to the question.

To evaluate the effectiveness of CA-RAG, two scenarios have been
designed. Scenario 1 involved experiments using widely adopted and recognized benchmark datasets, such
as TriviaQA, Natural Questions, AmbigQA and Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD). In this
context, the proposed CA-RAG method, combined with similarity measure (either cosine similarity or dot
product) between generated answers and chunks, achieved the highest F1-score in TriviaQA and AmbigQA. Scenario 2 tested CA-RAG robustness using a custom dataset comprising domain-specific and unstructured
documents. Results from automated and manual evaluations revealed that CA-RAG with post-processing
consistently outperformed traditional RAG. These findings highlight the critical role of post-processing
techniques and similarity measures in improving the accuracy and relevance of generated answers. CA-
RAG demonstrates strong potential as a reliable and versatile solution for Retrieval Augmented Generation
tasks across diverse datasets and domains. INDEX TERMS Context-aware retrieval augmented generation (CA-RAG), cosine similarity, dot product,
domain-specific tasks, large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

INTRODUCTION
Large Language Models (LLMs) are one of the most
important developments in Artificial Intelligence. LLMs like
ChatGPT [1], Claude [2], and Llama [3] can create text with
strong ‘‘understanding’’ and answers to questions in ways
that make sense to humans. These models use deep neural
networks trained on large amounts of text data, which allows
them to understand and produce human-like language. Many industries, including healthcare [4], [5], education [6], [7], [8], and finance [9], [10], [11], now use

queries outside their pretrained data or require domainspecific knowledge [12], [13]. Moreover, training and fine-tuning LLMs on specific
domain knowledge, which may contain sensitive and/or
private information, can expose and amplify vulnerabilities to
which such systems are prone, for instance prompt injection
attacks and several other adversarial techniques, which may

of computational resources [15], since fine-tuning strongly
relies on the availability of vast amounts of training data, and
this aspect is often limited in specialized domains. For these
reasons, fine-tuning may not be the best approach in all those
cases and contexts in which users, research entities, organizations and companies require to build LLM-based applications
and services for specific domain knowledge (products and/or
services manuals, internal/legal documentation etc.) which
may need frequent or continuous updates.

To address these challenges, the Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG) approach [16] has been considered. This
method improves LLM performance by retrieving relevant
information from pre-existing documents and using it to
generate answers. In this way, the RAG approach reduces
the need for exhaustive fine-tuning by leveraging up-todate information and specific domain knowledge, therefore
minimizing computational overhead and related costs. RAG
combines two processes:
1) Retrieval: The system retrieves relevant information
from external documents or sources.
2) Generation: The retrieved information is then used to
generate responses based on the query. By integrating these two processes, RAG is a scalable
and efficient solution that helps LLMs produce answers
that may result to be more reliable on domain-specific
questions.

This approach reduces the impact of hallucinations
and improves the factual accuracy by incorporating verified
external knowledge. In general, Lewis et al. RAG [16] works using the
‘‘Retrieve and Read’’ framework. This method improves
LLMs by adding external knowledge through steps such as
chunking data, storing it in vector format, and retrieving
relevant information based on similarity. However, existing
methods face several limitations [13], [17]. Actually, several
works have shown that proper selection of retrieval methods
can significantly enhance system performance [18], [19]. However, an incorrect selection of the retriever can significantly affect the outcomes of the generation process, and
may lead to missing key information in specific contexts. For instance, if the answer to a question is spread across
several different sections of a document (that may not be the
most semantically similar), or even in different documents,
a traditional RAG framework might not be able to retrieve
the most relevant chunks [20]. MOTIVATION AND MAIN OBJECTIVE
The use of RAG may provide several notable advantages
with respect to LLM fine tuning in different cases. First,
RAG is designed to use context for specific tasks, enabling
it to generate more relevant and tailored outputs in Question
and Answer tasks on specific domain knowledge. Therefore,
RAG allows to handle queries that go beyond the scope of
pre-trained models, since it excels at managing specialized
domain knowledge retrieved from external sources [21]. Moreover, RAG minimizes the risk of data leakage from
the pre-trained model, making it a reliable option for
maintaining privacy [22]. Furthermore, while fine-tuning
offers consistent performance, RAG provides a more efficient
and cost-effective alternative [23]. However, while efficient,
the traditional RAG approach introduces a critical bottleneck:
the overall answer quality heavily depends on the retriever’s
performance, as well as on the precision of the contextual
information used to generate answers [24]. Previous research
has identified computational complexity [21], [25] and
retrieval challenges [26], [27] as significant weaknesses in
current RAG. In particular, similarity measures used in the
retrieval stage may not effectively capture the contextual
relevance between a query and potentially relevant documents [28], [29]. Furthermore, dense vector representations,
such as document-level embedding models may not be
enough to capture important and semantically significant
content [24]. This may cause a semantic drift, where relevant
chunks are filtered out early, leading to incomplete or
inaccurate answers. Therefore, the traditional RAG approach
may often lead to the retrieval of documents or text
chunks which may be lexically similar but semantically
misaligned with the user’s expectations. Therefore, despite
its many advantages, traditional RAG has several significant
limitations. In order to address all the described issues,
this study proposes the Context-Aware Retrieval Augmented
Generation (CA-RAG) solution. PROPOSED METHOD AND CONTRIBUTIONS
The CA-RAG approach focuses on improving context awareness and mitigating retrieval precision issues by eliminating
the retrieval initial filter.

Rather than ranking raw documents
based on vector similarity to the query, our proposed method
consists in performing semantic chunking on documents
and providing all the extracted chunks to the LLM to
generate answers. Then, we rank generated answers using
similarity methods between the generated text and the
context, discarding answers whose similarity score undergoes
a certain threshold. This new approach moves the relevance
judgment to the LLM’s own interpretative ability, which can
be exploited on the whole unfiltered documentation. This
lays the foundation for obtaining more precise relevance
estimation and more complete answers (as outlined by
the results illustrated in the experimental section), since
the generated responses may reflect a deeper contextual
alignment with queries and user expectations. Therefore,
even if the proposed approach might be more expensive in
terms of response times than traditional RAG approaches,
the main focus of our work is to emphasize that there
are many real-world scenarios where answer accuracy and
completeness are much more important than performance.

This aspect is relevant in many specialized contexts such
as medical [30] or legal [31] domains, where response

accuracy and mitigation of spreading misinformation have
great importance [30], even at the expense of increased
computational cost, since users in these scenarios may
often prioritize the precision and reliability of answers over
minimizing response times. To summarize, the CA-RAG model introduces a straightforward yet effective method that uses similarity methods
evaluation to assess the relevance of responses generated
by the LLM to the given context. Unlike traditional RAG
methods that rely on top-k retrieval results, CA-RAG directly
evaluates the relevance of each retrieved chunk. This reduces
dependency on complex ranking systems and improves
retrieval accuracy. The following research objectives guide this study:
1) To propose the CA-RAG method and evaluate its
effectiveness without relying on the top-k retrieval
approach.
2) To implement Semantic Chunking and Fixed-Size
Chunking in the document chunking process, ensuring
that contextual information is preserved.
3) To propose the use of similarity methods evaluation
during the generation phase to improve the alignment
between retrieval and response generation. The paper is organized as follows: Section II provides
a review of state of the art RAG approaches, techniques
and implementations found in literature, focusing also on
comparative performance analysis. Section III introduces
the proposed CA-RAG model, detailing its components and
processes.

Section IV presents the experiments, results, and
analysis of the proposed model. Finally, Section V is left
for conclusions, outlining also potential directions for future
research. II. RELATED WORKS
Several studies suggest addressing RAG using different
approaches. Table 1 provides a comparative overview of the
current best practices in RAG that have been reviewed in the
literature. Pickett et al. [25] suggested a novel paradigm named
Dartboard. This study introduces the Dartboard algorithm,
which uses a simple measure of total information gain
for a specific query, and evaluates the effectiveness of
Dartboard on the RAG Benchmark. Their system was
compared with other methods including Oracle, Maximal
Marginal Relevance (MMR) Crosscoder, MMR Cossim, Knearest-neighbors (KNN) Crosscoder, KNN Cossim. The
highest Question Answer (QA) score for Dartboard (see
Table 1) is Exact String Match score of 85.6% (obtained
performing a string match of the response on a set of
correct answers, thus making each response as either correct
or incorrect).

Then, the highest Normalized Discounted
Cumulative Gain (NDCG) score is 0.975. An inherent
drawback of Dartboard is its computational complexity and
hyperparameter sensitivity. Yan et.al. [26] introduced a technique called Corrective
RAG (CRAG) aimed at improving robustness, automatic selfcorrection, and the effective exploitation of retrieved documents in RAG systems. CRAG begins with an initial retrieval
phase in which the user’s query is sent to a retriever to obtain
the top-k documents. Each resulting question-answer pair is
then evaluated by a T5-large-based retrieval evaluator, which
assigns a relevance score and classifies the pair into three
categories: correct, incorrect, or ambiguous. The corrective
procedure unfolds as follows: if the evaluator labels a pair
as correct, the corresponding document is split into small
fragments (‘‘knowledge strips’’); each strip is re-evaluated
and, if deemed irrelevant, discarded, whereas relevant strips
are merged into the internal knowledge store. If a pair is
judged as incorrect, all retrieved documents are considered
useless, the question is rewritten, and a web search is
performed; the newly retrieved information is filtered in the
same way as in the correct phase and stored as external
knowledge. If the evaluator deems a pair ambiguous, the
system combines internal and external knowledge to improve
robustness, after which the generator receives the query
together with the context selected in the foregoing steps. This approach consists of two variations, specifically CRAG
and Self-CRAG, with Self-CRAG incorporated the idea of
Self-RAG [32]. Mallen et al. assessed the effectiveness of
this approach by using major benchmark datasets including
PopQA [33] for short form production, Biographical [34]
for long form generation, PubHealth [35] for true-false
questions, and Arc-Challenge [36] for multiple choice. The
study reported accuracy scores for CRAG and Self-CRAG
using LLAMA2-fh-7b on PopQA, Biography, PubHealth,
and Arc-Challenge datasets (see Table 1). The best performance was achieved by Self-CRAG with accuracy of
69.1 on Biography dataset. The disadvantages of CRAG are
dependency on retrieval evaluators and potential bias in web
searches.

The method named LeanContext was proposed by
Arefeen et al. [37]. LeanContext methodology seeks to minimize the size of a context while maintaining accuracy by utilizing the original context. Experimental LeanContext studies
were performed on multiple datasets including the Arxiv
dataset [38], BBC dataset [39] and NarativeQA [40]. The
LeanContext framework utilizes the ROUGE method [41]
to evaluate its performance. The highest ROUGE score for
the Arxiv dataset is 0.2305, 0.5017 for the BBCNews, and
0.5244 for the NarrativeQA dataset. The effectiveness of
LeanContext, however, relies heavily on the proper training
of the reinforcement learning agent, which can be time
consuming.

The Rewrite-Retrieve-Read paradigm was introduced by
Ma et al. [17]. Rewrite first converts the original query into
one or more specific search queries. These queries are then
passed to the Retrieve phase, where they are sent to the
document index to fetch relevant articles that supply factual
context for generation. Finally, in the Read phase, the LLM
receives the relevant documents and the search query and

generates an answer to the user’s original query. Training
the rewriter happens in two stages. First step is Warmup: asks a large model such as GPT-4 to rewrite training
questions into sharper search queries. They keep only the
question–query pairs that lead to correct answers and use
these ‘‘pseudo-labels’’ to fine-tune a smaller rewriter model
(T5-large, 770 million parameters) so it can copy the same
query style. Second step is Reinforcement learning: Once the
rewriter is reasonably skilled, it starts writing its own queries. Each query goes to the retriever; the retrieved documents
are passed to a reader LLM, which produces an answer. The system gives a reward based on answer accuracy and
adds a KL-divergence penalty if the rewriter’s style drifts
too far from the original model. Using Proximal Policy
Optimization (PPO), the rewriter’s parameters are updated so
it more often creates queries that steer the reader toward the
correct answer.

Multiple datasets, including HotpotQA [42],
AmbigNQ [43], PopQA [33], MMNU [44], were used to
evaluate the suggested approach. The highest Exact Match
score of 45.72 was obtained for PopQA dataset. An inherent
limitation of the rewrite-retrieve-read approach is the issue of
balancing generalization and specialization. The approach developed by Shao et al. [27] was

Yet a single fact may appear in
several corpora. To avoid depending on one paragraph only,
the method generates several recitations through sampling
and forms a draft answer for each. The system then chooses
the final answer by majority vote. This strategy lowers the
chance of error caused by faulty recitation. The process

Natural Question [46], Trivia Question [47] and HotpotQA

direct questions. Updates are expensive, which is the primary
disadvantage of the Recite-Read method. Deng et al. [48], proposed a method called Credibility-
Aware Attention Modification (CrAM). CrAM is a method
that makes RAG systems aware of source credibility. It first identifies the attention heads in the LLM that
most strongly influence the model when it accidentally
relies on low-credibility documents to generate incorrect
answers, and then rescales those heads by multiplying each
token’s attention weight by the credibility score of its
source document—trusted sources keep their full weight,
while doubtful ones receive less. This adjustment steers the
model toward reliable information and away from possible
misinformation, improving answer accuracy without the need
to retrain the entire LLM. This approach was evaluated using
Trivia Question [47]. Effectiveness of the CrAM approach
lies in its user-friendly plug-and-play idea, which enhances its
usability. However, the limitation of CrAM is the granularity
of the credibility score. Wang et al. [21] introduced a technique named Relevance-
Aware Retrieval-Augmented (REAR) with the goal of developing a system that possesses a high level of self-awareness
on the applicability of resources in RAG systems. REAR
first operates by concatenating the user query with each
document and feeding the pair into a lightweight LLM,
which computes a relevance score indicating how closely the
document matches the query. This score is converted into a
guidance vector that is injected into the prompt: when the
score is high, the corresponding document is forwarded to
the generator; when it is low, the LLM relies on its internal
knowledge to produce the answer. For noise robustness, the
model is trained jointly on a binary match/no-match signal
and a ranking objective that orders documents by relevance,
and it is further exposed to noisy documents so that it can still
answer correctly even under perturbations. Evaluation of the
REAR approach was conducted on many datasets including
Natural Questions [46], TriviaQA [47], WebQuestion [49],
dan SquaD [50]. While REAR offers benefits in terms
of effective training methods and robustness to external
retrieval of different retrieval capacities, the drawback is
the computational complexity and lack of granularity in
attention. Glass et al. [51] proposed a new approach called Re2G
(Retrieve, Rerank, Generation).

It works in three steps. First,
a dual-retrieval stage uses Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR)
and BM25 to gather 100 candidate documents. Next, a BERT
cross-encoder reranks these candidates by scoring how well
each document matches the query and keeps the top-k pieces
of evidence. Finally, the chosen passages are passed to
a BART-large generator, which produces the answer. The
authors tested Re2G on several datasets, including T-REx,
Natural Questions, FEVER, and Wizard of Wikipedia. The
method improves the accuracy of document selection through
the reranker and remains modular, but the extra reranking step
also adds latency. Methods such as Dartboard [25] and REAR [21] achieved
strong performance, however introduced high computational overhead, limiting their practicality in real-world
applications. Similarly, methods like CRAG [26] and
ITER-RETGEN [27] depend heavily on retrieval accuracy,
which can reduce their effectiveness in handling diverse
queries.

RAG works in three main stages: indexing, retrieving, and
generating. Figure 1 represent the RAG workflow. In the indexing stage, documents are split into smaller
chunks, which are transformed into vector representations
using an embedding function.

In this study, we used Sentence-
BERT [52], a transformer-based model that is designed
to produce sentence-level embeddings with high semantic
accuracy. These vector representations are saved in a vector
database to make retrieval process more efficient in the next
steps. When a user makes a query, the first operation performed
by the system is the retrieving stage. In this phase, the
question is processed using the same embedding technique
as in indexing, converting it into a vector representation. A semantic search using similarity measures (e.g., cosine
similarity) is then performed between the vectorized query
and the vectors stored in the database to find the most relevant
chunks. The similarity between each chunk and the query
is calculated, and the results are sorted to select the top-k
chunks. In the generating stage, the retrieved chunks are combined
with the user’s original question and used as input to a
large language model (LLM). The LLM creates a clear and
appropriate response, combining the external information
from the retrieved documents with its internal knowledge to
give accurate and useful answers. CONTEXT AWARE RETRIEVAL AUGMENTED

IV. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULT
In this study, we conducted experiments to evaluate the
performance of the proposed CA-RAG method in two
different scenarios. The first scenario used the TriviaQA [47],
Natural Question [46], AmbigQA [43], and Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) [50] benchmark dataset,
while the second scenario involved a custom dataset with
questions divided into general, specific, and out-of-context
categories. We made a comparative evaluation among our
proposed approach and multiple RAG configurations using
different retrieval setups: RAG with MiniLM as embedding
model, RAG with Contriever as embedding model, and
additional two configurations applying a Reranker to both of
the two aforementioned embedding setups.

This section is organized into five subsections to give a

adopted evaluation metrics. (B) Dataset Preparation explains the source datasets and the

used for RAG, including the maximum chunk size, the

used. (D) CA-RAG Setup describes the experiment settings used
in the creation of CA-RAG, both from the post
processing performed on both scenarios. (E) Experimental Result presents the outcomes in tables
and figures, making it easier to understand and also
interpreting the results and how they relate to the
research objectives. EVALUATION METHODS
In this study, different evaluation methods have been used
for the two experimental scenarios, in order to assess the
performance of the proposed approach. For Scenario 1, we use BERTScore [55] as the main metric.

BERTScore evaluates the similarity between the generated
answer and the ground-truth answer by comparing their
contextual embeddings. It calculates Precision, Recall, and
F1-score using a pre-trained language model as its backbone,
ensuring a semantic understanding of the text instead of just
matching exact tokens. In Scenario 2, the evaluation focuses on the system’s ability
to handle specific, general, and out-of-context questions
under more realistic conditions, that is including real
documents, such as scientific articles, in order to assess the
capability of the systems of handling much longer contextual
information, where only a part of it may be relevant to specific
questions. Unlike Scenario 1, we used a manual evaluation
method in this case. In Scenario 2, the evaluation was carried out at the
chunk level and the question level. This means that human
evaluators assessed whether the system generated a correct
or incorrect answer based on the result of the generated
answer obtained from the LLMs model, according to several
conditions. As a result, for each topic with n questions and
m retrieved chunks, the evaluation required assessing n × m
question-chunk pairs. Each pair was evaluated individually,
making the assessment more fine-grained and sensitive to
context. The manual evaluation for Scenario 2 followed these
criteria: a generated answer which is found to be correct for
specific or general questions has been classified as a True
Positive (TP); when the system provides an incorrect answer
for specific and general questions, this is classified as a False
Positive (FP); the case in which the system correctly responds
with ‘‘no context provided’’ for out-of-context questions is
classified as a True Negative (TN); finally, if the system
provides an answer different from ‘‘no context provided’’ for
out-of-context questions, this is classified as a False Negative
(FN). The choice of producing ‘‘no context provided’’ as an
answer to out-of-context questions has been made in order
to handle those cases where the LLMs generate answers
based on their internal knowledge, which may lead to
hallucinations, and this frequently occurs in domain-specific
scenarios, where general knowledge provided by the LLM
may be inadequate or even inaccurate. Therefore, we intentionally adopted the conservative strategy of returning ‘‘no
context provided’’ when the retrieved context does not
contain relevant or sufficient evidence to answer the query. TP, FP, TN and FN metrics were finally used to compute
overall Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score. To ensure
reliability and consistency, the manual evaluation has been
conducted by 1–3 domain experts, providing a thorough and
expert-level assessment of the system’s performance. DATASET PREPARATION

includes Question Answer pairs with passages taken from

SQuAD is a dataset built

This

requiring additional reasoning. In contrast, the general
questions follow an abstractive approach, where the questions
are formulated more broadly, and answers may either be
directly stated in the article or require a higher level of

In the pre-processing stage, several steps are performed
to improve the quality of the used dataset. The first step is
removing escape sequences, where special characters like
\n or \\n are replaced with spaces. This ensures the text
readability is not disturbed by unnecessary symbols. Next,
extra spaces between words are removed. Backslashes (\)
and slashes (/) are also removed. Repeated characters, such
as punctuation marks like ‘‘!!!’’ or ‘‘...’’, are replaced with a
single instance. In addition, non-breaking spaces like \xa0 are replaced
with regular spaces, which helps clean invisible special
characters. Square brackets, such as [ and ]. Hyphenated
words split with spaces are corrected and joined back to form
a single word. Lastly, escape characters are cleaned again if
required, ensuring the text is free of all formatting issues.

CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
This work introduces a novel approach for Retrieval
Augmented Generation called Context-Aware Retrieval Augmented Generation (CA-RAG), which adapts the ‘‘retrieve
and read’’ framework used by traditional RAG while
eliminating vector representations and the top-k process in
the retrieve stage. The approach incorporates a similarity
evaluator after the generative phase to address hallucination
issues and enhance contextual relevance. The choice of either
cosine similarity or dot product between the embedding of the
generated answer and the context is a reliable proxy to assess
chunks relevance. However, this may not always be the case,
particularly for queries requiring abstract reasoning or multihop answers, as well as when chunks contain both relevant
and irrelevant content. In Scenario 1, we compared our proposed method, CA-
RAG, with RAG using MiniLM, RAG using Contriever,
and RAG with Rerank applied to both the embedding
configurations. We applied both semantic chunking and
fixed-size chunking to four well-established benchmark
datasets: TriviaQA, NaturalQA, SQuAD, and AmbigQA. We found that different chunking methods led to different
results.With semantic chunking, RAG with Rerank achieved
better performance than our proposed method. This may be
due to a more effective selection of ‘‘optimal’’ chunks, which
helps retrieve more relevant answers. In addition, the use
of semantic chunking may have played a significant role in
helping Rerank perform better in selecting the most suitable
chunk for answer generation. However, when using fixed-size
chunking, our method outperformed the others. Fixed-size
chunking provided better results for our method because it
may ensure that each chunk has a consistent length, allowing

the encoder to work more efficiently. In contrast, semantic
chunking may produce uneven chunk sizes or split the context
in ways that reduce the relevance of retrieved content, which
can lower performance on some datasets. On the other hand,
Contriever combined with semantic chunking performed
better than our method because its retrieval process is more
effective at selecting semantically meaningful content to
generate answers. In comparison, our List CA-RAG method
with either cosine similarity or dot product relies on matching
generated responses with context, which may be less precise
in semantic alignment.

In scenario 2, the evaluation focused on testing the system’s
ability to handle specific, general, and outside-the-context
questions under more realistic conditions. Unlike Scenario 1,
this scenario used a manual evaluation method based on
chunk-level assessments and question-level assessment on
a custom dataset built with whole scientific papers, thus
providing longer and less structured context. For each topic,
multiple questions have been paired with retrieved chunks,
and human evaluators judged whether the generated answer
was correct, incorrect, or appropriately left unanswered when
no relevant context was available. The results showed that
CA-RAG with post-processing significantly outperformed
both RAG and CA-RAG without post-processing, achieving
F1-score of 0.9408 on semantic chunking, and 0.94 on fixed
chunking. This strong performance is closely related to the
method’s ability to detect correctly when there is no relevant
information in a section, resulting in a high number of True
Negatives (TN) and fewer False Positives (FP) and False
Negative (FN). In contrast, models without post-processing
often produced hallucinated answers, as they lacked a
mechanism to filter out irrelevant chunks. These results
highlight the importance of post-processing techniques in
generative QA, particularly when operating in complex,
open-domain environments where questions may not always
align with the retrieved content. The experiments also
demonstrate that CA-RAG with post-processing outperforms
existing methods, making it a reliable solution for Retrieval
Augmented Generation tasks. Since our approach provides
all the chunks to the LLM without the retrieval stage (as in
traditional RAG), it may be most practical for moderated size
corpora, in those real-world contexts where answer accuracy
and completeness are paramount. The proposed CA-RAG has shown a higher average
per-question time than RAG/RAG-Rerank, with 262.7s
under semantic chunking and 2289.5s under fixed-size
chunking. The overhead is notably smaller with semantic
chunking, which in conclusion can be considered as the most
representative approach, since it produced the best overall
performances in Scenario 2. Moreover, the processing times
of our best CA-RAG configuration remains substantially
lower than the time a human expert would require to read
specialized documentation and produce similarly accurate
answers. Finally, our method produced significantly higher
performances in Scenario 2 than the best RAG model (i.e. RAG with reranking), at a slightly higher computational cost
per query (about 262s for CA-RAG with semantic chunking,
versus 85s for RAG with reranking). For future work, the
integration of a chain-of-taught query algorithm, as proposed
by [65], will be explored to further enhance the retrieval and
generation stages.
